extracted.intended_audience: pianists, piano teachers, and advanced piano students seeking technical and interpretive guidance
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and interpretive standards for piano playing and pedagogy: technique, practice methods, interpretation, teaching principles, and stagecraft as described by established concert pianists and teachers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety of tone color
rubrics_metrics.description: Colors mean so much ... We can make as wonderful combinations with them as ever the painters do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a rich palette of tonal shades (e.g., shades of red for tenderness, yellows for gaiety); tone-color variety is essential and pianists who neglect it miss much beauty. Illustrate different colors at the keyboard (staccato for brightness, legato for warmth).

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual and artistic phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual and artistic phrasing is one of four requisites for the pianist who would make an artistic success in public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop personal phrasing that expresses the piece's meaning—be a 'law to yourself' in phrasing when sufficiently immersed in the work rather than slavishly following printed marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: True feeling (emotional integrity)
rubrics_metrics.description: True feeling is essential; no sympathy with dry, mechanical performance where every effect is coldly calculated beforehand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow mood and genuine emotion to shape performances; expect differing interpretations each time because feelings vary. Avoid uniform, prepackaged renditions—mechanical uniformity kills inspiration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal magnetism / stage presence
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal magnetism is listed among the four necessary things for public artistic success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop stage persona and presence (gestures, carriage, charisma) as part of communicating with an audience; presentation complements technical and interpretive skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect the limits of printed markings
rubrics_metrics.description: Editing of piano music is extremely inadequate—dots, lines, dashes and accents cannot give a true idea of interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use printed dynamics and articulations as guides but realize there are 'infinite shadings' between piano and forte; rely on internalized understanding and imagination to supply unnotated nuances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make climaxes pianissimo (use tonal surprises)
rubrics_metrics.description: In lyric playing, instead of making the highest point the loudest, make it soft so 'the thing you did not expect has happened'—constant tonal surprises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create surprise and expressive interest by shaping crescendos so that the perceived climax is softer or smoothed—prioritize unexpected tonal coloring over predictable loudness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn tone production from singers and opera
rubrics_metrics.description: The human voice is the greatest of all instruments; the player can have no more convincing lesson in tone production and tone coloring than from a great emotional singer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend opera and study great singers to learn phrasing, color, light and shade, and emotional action; apply vocal models to piano tone and coloring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid cut-and-dried, mechanical performances
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not strive to do every effect the same way each time; the true artist will never give a mechanical performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value spontaneity and variability; recognize that repeating identical performances signals lack of feeling. Allow interpretive freedom while staying within musical bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breath control for pianists
rubrics_metrics.description: Breath control: respiration must be easy and natural; in fortissimo and difficult passages, lips must be kept closed and respiration taken through the nostrils.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate natural breathing habits even at the keyboard (mental/physical breathing) to support phrasing and sustained effort; treat breath as a tool for musical line and stamina.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful hand position and touch
rubrics_metrics.description: With pupils I am very particular about hand position and touch. The ends of the fingers must be firm, but otherwise the hand, wrist and arm, from the shoulder, are all relaxed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insist on firm finger endings, relaxed wrists and arms; monitor and correct hand/wrist/arm alignment and tension in lessons; finger joints should be firm especially the third joint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dissect and analyze details of a composition
rubrics_metrics.description: In teaching a composition, I am immensely careful and particular about each note. Everything is dissected and analyzed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work methodically through a piece, isolating and correcting issues at the note and phrase level before assembling the full stage-ready interpretation ('stage setting, the actors, the lights, and the colors').

rubrics_metrics.name: Early technical training and gymnastics
rubrics_metrics.description: Stretching and gymnastic exercises were invented and used early in training and are splendid if done the right way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include targeted stretching and physical exercises for hands/arms early in training, performed correctly to avoid harm; incorporate them into daily routine for physical preparedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extensive technical exercises in all keys and touches
rubrics_metrics.description: There were 580 technical exercises ... Everything must be played in all keys, and with every possible variety of touch—legato, staccato, half-staccato, and so on; also, with all kinds of shading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice a wide catalogue of technical drills in all keys and articulations; transpose etudes and exercises so both hands receive equal training; variety of touch and shading is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transposing practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Each etude must also be transposed ... whatever I could perform at all, I was able to play in any key.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train the habit of transposing pieces and etudes regularly to develop musical flexibility and key-independent command.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-criticism and listening
rubrics_metrics.description: Part of my training consisted in being shown how to criticize myself. I learned to listen, to be critical, to judge my own work; ... the earlier this can be learned the better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach students to assess their playing critically and independently; develop the habit of listening analytically and correcting shortcomings without sole reliance on teacher feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relaxation as the secret of power
rubrics_metrics.description: The secret of power lies in relaxation; power is relaxation ... It is really mental relaxation, for one has to think it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate controlled relaxation (mental and physical) to achieve power without strain; avoid 'flopping'—relax exactly where needed and nowhere else so endurance and tone improve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seat/stool height and posture
rubrics_metrics.description: I am particular about the seat I use at the piano, as I sit lower than most amateurs, who in general are apt to sit too high.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust stool/pedal height so the player sits low enough for comfortable hand position and efficient action; experiment to find ergonomic posture that enables even scales and arpeggios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scales and arpeggios as ongoing practice
rubrics_metrics.description: I still believe in scales and arpeggios ... I practise technic daily ... When on tour I try to give one hour a day to it, not more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain regular scale/arpeggio practice to 'overhaul' technic weekly; practice different touches (legato, staccato); daily but measured practice preserves condition without overwork.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hand obliquity/slant for arpeggios
rubrics_metrics.description: I slant the hand considerably across the keys ... this oblique position is more comfortable, and the hand can accommodate itself to the intervals of the arpeggio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an oblique hand position to facilitate smooth arpeggios and thumb passages; accept individual ergonomic differences (even if elbow 'sticks out') when they aid evenness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular overhauling of technique
rubrics_metrics.description: I have to overhaul my technic once or twice a week, to see that everything is all right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Periodically audit and correct technical habits; select focused areas (scales, arpeggios, octaves) for maintenance to prevent deterioration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measured approach to velocity
rubrics_metrics.description: I never work for that special thing [velocity] as some do. I seldom practise with great velocity, for it interferes with clearness. I prefer to play more slowly, giving the greatest attention to clearness and good tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize clarity, tone and control over raw speed. Develop speed only after achieving clarity at slower tempos; avoid sacrificing musicality for velocity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use metronome judiciously
rubrics_metrics.description: I approve of the metronome to cultivate the sense of rhythm in those who are lacking ... I sometimes use it myself, just to see the difference between the mechanical rhythm and the musical rhythm—for they are not always the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ the metronome as a training tool to build steady rhythm, but compare and adjust for musical flexibility; do not let mechanical pulse override musical phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Octave development by gradual, frequent practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The only alternative [for octaves] is to work constantly at them ... A little at a time, in frequent doses, ought in six months to work wonders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop octaves progressively with short, regular practice sessions to avoid strain, especially for small hands; physical cross-training (e.g., rowing) may help wrist development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study concertos with full orchestral score
rubrics_metrics.description: In studying such a work, for piano and orchestra, I must not only know my own part but all the other parts—what each instrument is doing. I always study a concerto with the orchestral score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn concerto repertoire by consulting the orchestral score so the pianist understands context, texture, and interplay with orchestra; this informs phrasing and coordination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technic must continue alongside pieces
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical study must continue along the whole course, hand in hand with piece playing; technic for its own sake, outside the playing of compositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sustain technical drills even at advanced stages; never treat technique as something finished—keep it in working order through ongoing focused practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arched hand position and firm finger joints with loose wrists
rubrics_metrics.description: I teach arched hand position, and ... Two things are of supreme importance: namely, firm finger joints and loose wrists; these must be insisted on from the very beginning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish arched hand, firm finger joints (no wobbling) and supple wrists early; occasional firm wrists may be used intentionally for effect, but not as a habit of weakness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beginners must learn 'according to rule' first
rubrics_metrics.description: The beginner must go according to rule, until he has thoroughly mastered the rules. He must not attempt eccentricities seen in artists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach foundational, safe technique before imitating advanced artists' idiosyncrasies; artists' apparent eccentricities result from experience and should not be mimicked by novices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation: imagination, character, and theme prominence
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpretation: arouse the imagination of the student first ... speak of the character of the piece ... opening theme should be made prominent to arrest attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guide students to conceive the piece's character (e.g., largo = serious) and to shape themes and phrases imaginatively; emphasize variety and individuality in interpretive choices rather than strict adherence to metronome markings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pianissimo requires strength, not weakness
rubrics_metrics.description: Pianissimo is one of the later things to teach ... A true pianissimo is not the result of weakness but of strength.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop control and strength before attempting genuine soft dynamics; avoid flabbiness by teaching controlled, supported quiet playing as an advanced skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmony study as prerequisite to pedaling and analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: One thing a teacher should insist upon ... the pupil should study harmony. He should have a practical working knowledge of keys, chords, and progressions ... Without this knowledge, my words about the use of the pedals are as so much Greek to him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require students to learn harmony and chord analysis to inform pedaling, phrasing and structural understanding; simple composition/orchestration knowledge is helpful but not mandatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor teaching to individual pupil differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Each pupil presents a different problem as to physical formation of hand and body, intelligence and talent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess each student's physical and intellectual profile and adapt teaching accordingly; prioritize obedient, diligent students over raw talent that resists disciplined work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finger action for beginners and initial development
rubrics_metrics.description: Finger action is an absolute essential in playing the piano. We must have finger development. In the beginning, the fingers are to be raised, though not too high.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach deliberate finger action early to build strength and clarity, then reduce visible motion as control improves; finger lifts help initial development even if later playing appears economical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate keyboard action/weight for children
rubrics_metrics.description: Children ought to have a keyboard adapted to their little delicate muscles, with action much less heavy than two ounces ... If they should attempt to use my instrument with its heavy action, they would lame the hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide instruments with lighter touch for young students and gradually increase action weight as strength develops to prevent injury and ensure correct technique formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strengthening weak finger joints quickly
rubrics_metrics.description: When a new pupil comes to me the first thing we do is to get the hand into correct position, and the fingers rounded and firm ... If the pupil is intelligent and quick, this can be accomplished in a few weeks; sometimes it takes several months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address weak finger joints immediately through positional correction and strengthening drills at the keyboard (or table) until rounded firmness is achieved before tackling demanding repertoire.
